segments.translation_text: Genuine wisdom is certainty of the relationship between the ultimate (or definitive) teachings which carry the meaning of ultimate suchness, and the relative (or interpretive) teachings which carry the meaning that guides beings. Understanding this dispels the doubts of those who are disciples; develops devotion to the Buddha’s doctrine; and increases from height to height the special virtuous qualities of the two accumulations within one’s own and others’ minds. The Ornament states:

segments.translation_text: The opposite of wisdom that should be discarded is ignorance. The antidote is realization of the selflessness of phenomena, through which one possesses primordial wisdom of non-conceptualization of the three cycles. The outcome that is a temporary result is wisdom that cuts all the doubts of other beings which fulfills all their wishes. The ultimate result is placing sentient beings in the nirvana of one of the three vehicles according to their motivation. Thus, beings are completely matured through the four dharmas.

segments.translation_text: Meaningful nature is to understand and completely classify all knowledge exactly and entirely. The meaningful cause is insight wisdom which arises based on calm abiding. The meaningful result is complete liberation from every type of defilement. Meaningful action is the ability to teach correctly and to engage in right livelihood. Meaningful possession means that good qualities are possessed as described, such as "Wisdom is exalted among all other dharmas,” etc.

segments.translation_text: Concerning the ultimate, there are two types: the countable ultimate and the final uncountable ultimate. The countable ultimate is the mere rejection of arising, etc., which is the negation of the existence of anything. The uncountable final ultimate is the suchness of peace away from all existence, non-existence, etc. Thus, there are two types of ultimate.

segments.translation_text: The inseparability of the realm of reality and the ultimate good qualities cannot be seen, however it is seriously incorrect to believe that since one has not perceived it, no such thing exists, and to cling to that belief. In general, the mere fact that something is not perceived cannot be the method of ascertaining its nonexistence. In this case, the realm of reality cannot be seen because it is obscured by temporary stains. Through meditation on the path, gradually the ultimate will become more and more directly clear. segments.translation_text: Brahma: The followers of Brahma are called Vedics. They are also known as practitioners of sacrifice. In their tradition, the four Vedas are uncompounded phenomena that are permanent, like space. Their belief is not logically correct, because they believe that their school originated from four-faced Brahma, and yet they also state that later it came from recitation of the Vedas by Brahmans.

segments.translation_text: They also say that the four castes arose from the four parts of Brahma’s body: from the mouth appeared the Brahmans; from the shoulders appeared the kings; from the thighs appeared the nobles; and from the legs appeared the ordinary castes. These beliefs are logically inconsistent because they also believe that all were born from one god. If that were the case, all four castes would be of the same race, as they were born from a single god, like sons born from a single father.

segments.translation_text: Vishnu: There are various schools of the followers of Vishnu: Nayaka, logicians, singers of songs as a spiritual path, followers of Ishvara, Shivaites, and practitioners of sexual activity as a spiritual path. segments.translation_text: If Vishnu and Ishvara were the creators of everything, as the followers of Vishnu believe, this would imply that Vishnu and Ishvara would experience the result of every action. If this position is accepted, they would not be independent, because in the conventional sense, there is no creator other than interdependent arising.

segments.translation_text: They believe that after death, the mind does not take another body in the next life. Therefore, as there are no past or future lives, they believe that whatever methods make one comfortable in this life are sufficient. If this belief were correct, it would imply that trees, which are also the combination of earth and other elements, would have sense organs and mental consciousness. However, as this an outrageous implication, their position is demonstrated to be false.

segments.translation_text: Jains: There is another school that is called by various names: school of exhaustion, naked ones, Jains, those inclined toward offering, and skyclothed. In their tradition, life is permanent and equal to the length of the body. This is illogical, because by implication, life would be shortened if a limb were amputated. It would also imply that when people become taller or shorter, or gain and lose weight, their life would become longer or shorter. This position contradicts their statement of permanence.

segments.translation_text: They also believe that trees, grains, flowers, and fruit have life because they drink water from their roots. This is illogical because if plants had life, then a stalk of sugar cane which is cut into several segments would have as many lives as there are segments of sugar cane. They may reply that the life dwells contracted in one of those segments and the other segments have no life. If that were the case, it would imply that planting the other segments in the ground would not produce sprouts, etc.

segments.translation_text: The Vaivashika believe that the self is indescribable, neither permanent nor impermanent, yet truly existent. This analysis is inconsistent and illogical because if the self were the consciousness, it would imply that it is impermanent for immediately after the consciousness perceives a vase, it can perceive another material such as fabric. If the self were matter, it would imply that it would be unable to experience any pain or pleasure. Therefore, their position is illogical.
segments.translation_html: The Vaivashika believe that the self is indescribable, neither permanent nor impermanent, yet truly existent. This analysis is inconsistent and illogical because if the self were the consciousness, it would imply that it is impermanent57I.e., characterized by change. for immediately after the consciousness perceives a vase, it can perceive another material such as fabric. If the self were matter, it would imply that it would be unable to experience any pain or pleasure. Therefore, their position is illogical.

segments.translation_text: As this explains, the Mind Only School rejects the non-Buddhist belief that there is a self that possesses limbs or branches. They also reject the belief of the two Shravaka schools that atoms have material existence. Instead, they believe that like the perceptions of a dream, external objects do not exist in reality, but due to habitual tendencies, objects are merely perceived. The consciousness, which lacks both subject and object, ultimately exists in a self-seeing and self-illuminating manner.

segments.translation_text: As this explains, non-Buddhists believe in a self that has multiple branches. Shravakas believe that external objects have a certain subtle true existence. Also, the Mind-Only School believes that the consciousness alone truly exists. The Middle Way does not believe that any of these exist. Instead, the Middle Way follows the middle sermon of the Buddha which taught that if analyzed, all relative phenomena have no inherent nature, although they are perceived by the conventional consciousness, because they are beyond singular or plural nature, like the appearance of a lotus in space.

segments.translation_text: The Middle Way is also based on the last sermon, which taught that phenomena are free from the four extremes. They are free of the extreme of existence because they are empty of temporary stains; free of the extreme of non-existence because they are not empty of the nature of the realm of reality; free from both existence and non-existence because these are fundamentally contradictory; and because of rejecting that, they are also free of the extreme of neither. Thus although this can be perceived by ultimate primordial wisdom, it is free from the four extremes.

segments.translation_text: Ordinary worldly beings cling to the self as "I” and "my.” The noble beings of the Shravaka path realize personal selflessness. Prateka Buddhas who dwell secluded and alone in peace realize both personal selflessness and the subjective half of phenomenal selflessness. Wise Bodhisattvas realize both personal selflessness and phenomenal selflessness. Naturally arisen perfectly and fully enlightened Buddhas realize all knowledge. Their wisdom, which measures ultimate reality, is more subtle and profound and goes from height to height.

segments.translation_text: The wisdom of ordinary childlike sentient beings is like searching with the hand for an object on a dark night. The wisdom of the hearers and solitary Buddhas is like searching with a small lamp in hand for an object in the dense darkness of a cave. The wisdom of Mahayana practitioners, who possess great compassion, is like directly perceiving something in the daylight. The view of each of the schools is successively more exalted than each of the previous ones, so adopt their wisdom in this manner. The Ornament states:

segments.translation_text: As this explains, the Dharma of the Buddha is taught based on four different schools. Understanding this, gradually adopt the views of the more exalted ones. According to the view of the Mind Only school, reject belief in the true existence of external phenomena as held by the Shravaka tradition. According to the view of the Middle Way Without Perception, reject the view that only the mind truly exists. According to the view of the Middle Way With Perception, reject the view of the Middle Way Without Perception, and realize the realm of reality, which is beyond the activities of the four extremes. The Lankara Sutra states:

segments.translation_text: Relative phenomena are empty of subject and object. The ultimate realm of reality is not empty because it is characterized by complete freedom from the extremes of existence and non-existence. The nature of emptiness pervades all phenomena, so therefore emptiness is not a separate entity. Phenomena are compounded, yet their nature is uncompounded and their characteristics are not the same, therefore, they are not a singular entity; their characteristic is complete freedom from themselves and from other.

segments.translation_text: From the point of view of never changing to another form, emptiness is termed suchness. From the point of view of seeing perfectly without error, it is termed extreme perfection. From the point of view of being the state of cessation of all signs of activity, it is termed signlessness. From the point of view of being the object of experience of the holy ones’ noble primordial wisdom, it is termed the ultimate. From the point of view of being the cause of the arising of all noble Dharmas, it is termed the realm of reality.

segments.translation_text: Contaminated suchness is the state of samsara with all of the defilements. Uncontaminated suchness is the state of nirvana that is completely pure. Thus there are two classifications of suchness. Though the contaminated can be transformed into the uncontaminated, its own inherent nature never changes.

segments.translation_text: Inner emptiness is devoid of internal sense organs, such as the eye, etc. which are the experiencers. Outer emptiness is devoid of the external objects of the sense organs such as form which are the objects of experience, etc. Outer and inner emptiness is devoid of a main torso or body for the outer and inner sense organs. Great emptiness is devoid of the vast world as a container or base.

Emptiness without beginning and end is devoid of the beginning and end of samsara which the mind does not give up. Emptiness with nothing to abandon is devoid of the performance of inexhaustible virtue even after entering non-remaining nirvana. Emptiness of nature is devoid of the stainless nature which is purified of contamination.

segments.translation_text: If defilements could be eliminated without meditating the antidote, all sentient beings would become liberated without effort. To do this, exert oneself in meditation with an understanding of the profound meaning of emptiness.

segments.translation_text: The good quality of vastness is realization of the suchness of ultimate truth which is empty of both personal and phenomena self and completely realizes all the endless forms of knowable phenomena. The good quality of freedom from materialism is not being attached to the two extremes of samsara and nirvana. The good quality of great purpose is placing disciples in one of the three types of enlightenment according to their motivation. The good quality of inexhaustibility is continuing without ceasing, even in the state of nirvana without remainder, in order to completely hold all sentient beings through great compassion.

segments.translation_text: The Sons of the Jinas always realize the suchness of all knowable phenomena. If mental attachment does not arise toward nirvana, what need to mention toward samsara? Even that primordial wisdom alone places all beings in the three types of enlightenment. As that primordial wisdom completely accepts sentient beings, it is inexhaustible in the world.

segments.translation_html: Upon a foundation of understanding the non-dual perfection of wisdom, in order to attain the result which is an understanding of the Tathagata’s perfection of wisdom, meditate the profound perfection of wisdom as a path. For this purpose one should correctly study and contemplate authentic texts which teach the perfection of wisdom. Wisdom will develop gradually from study, contemplation, and meditation, and unsurpassable enlightenment, which is the ultimate among all attainments, will be achieved. Nagarjuna’s Jewel Garland states:

''A Commentary on Shantideva's Engaging in the Conduct of the Bodhisattvas Written by Sazang Mati Panchen: Known as An Extremely Clear Illumination of the Meaning of the Text''. segments.translation_text: Objects that are experienced by the consciousness are relative truth. Objects that are experienced by the primordial wisdom are ultimate truth. These are sequentially known as temporarily infallible, like the realization of the childlike, and then forever infallible, like the realization of the Noble Ones.

segments.translation_text: All phenomena can be classified into the two truths. In the world, there are two types of people who perceive these two truths. Those who realize that the nature of phenomena is emptiness and meditate on it are known as practitioners. Those who hold the deluded perception of phenomena as real are known as ordinary beings.

segments.translation_text: For instance, the Shravaka Vaivashika tradition believes that all knowable things (the five foundations) have material substance. This view is outshone by the Sutrantika tradition which believes that form, mind, and mental product exist in reality. All compounded phenomena without substance and all uncompounded phenomena are merely labels. They do not exist as material substances. Thus the Vaivashika view is outshone by the view of the Sutrantika.

[[Texts/Bodhicaryāvatāra/Verses/9.5|Verse 9.5]]  ·  [[Translation Memory:001-Tsadra-BCA-Root-Padmakara/714|Verse tm]]
segments.translation_html:
Worldly beings perceive matter
And conceive it as reality,
Not as a magical apparition.
Here practitioners and worldly beings disagree.

segments.wylie: don dam par chos thams cad kyi gnas lugs stong pa nyid yin yang kun rdzob tsam du rnal 'byor pa dang phal ba gnyis ka yang ni snang la rang bzhin med par 'dod pa'i dpe sgyu ma dang rmi lam dang smig rgyu la sogs pas 'bras bu mtho ris dang thar pa thob pa'i don du rgyu bsod nams kyi tshogs la 'jug pa na/_bden med du ma spyad par las rgyu 'bras la yid ches par bya ba'i phyir/_phung po dang khams dang skye mched rnams bstan pa la/
segments.translation_text: The ultimate nature of all phenomena is emptiness, yet on the merely relative level, both practitioners and ordinary beings do mutually agree about examples that are perceivable yet lack inherent nature such as magical apparitions, dreams, mirages, and the like. When the accumulation of merit is engaged in as a cause to attain the result of higher rebirth and liberation, the aggregates, elements, sense organs and their objects were taught in order that everything would not be treated as lacking truth, and to encourage trust in the law of cause and effect.

segments.translation_text: Disagreement occurs here, when practitioners and ordinary beings measure the truth of material reality. Under analysis, practitioners cannot find any material that has true substance. The things that are perceived when analysis is lacking have no inherent nature, like a magical apparition. Therefore, disagreement arises in their views.

segments.translation_text: This demonstrates that the subject is also invalid. Forms, sounds, etc. do not truly exist as they manifest in the consensus of worldly people. They are a misconception. Therefore, the consensus of worldly beings is not real; it is false and deceptive.

segments.translation_html:
For practitioners, there is no fault in the relative.
In comparison to worldly beings, they see suchness.
Otherwise, their realization of the certainty of the impurity of the female body
Would be outshone by the worldly.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: Although worldly beings cannot see this, yogis’ analysis of the nature of reality as the four truths split into sixteen categories, sees that all relative compounded phenomena are momentarily impermanent. Therefore, this is not false or contradictory, because worldly beings believe that compounded phenomena are permanent, which is a misconception. Compared to that view, even seeing phenomena as momentary is seeing them as suchness.

segments.translation_text: Therefore, worldly beings’ belief that compounded phenomena are permanent does not outshine yogis’ realization that they are impermanent. If it did outshine it, it would imply that worldly beings’ perception that women’s bodies are pure would outshine yogis’ realization arising from meditation and pure conduct that women’s bodies are impure. As this is an outrageous statement, your position is refuted.

segments.translation_text: The fact that something is like a magical apparition does not contradict its being a field of merit. Just as the Buddha is a magical apparition, from the acts of offering, serving, and veneration, a heap of merit like a magical apparition arises, increases, and develops. From this, the relative rupakaya is magnificently accomplished. The merit accumulated in this way is the same as for those who hold the materialist belief that the Buddha truly exists, and believe that from acts of offering, service, and veneration, a heap of merit that has true material form arises.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: The statement that sentient beings are like a magical apparition does not contradict the process of rebirth in the next life. Just as magical apparitions of humans or cities are maintained as long as conditions such as mantra and magical substances are gathered together, so sentient beings continue to take rebirth as long as samsaric conditions such as ignorance, desire, and the rest are gathered.

Possessing an illusory mind,
Merit and sin arise.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: If one benefits a magical apparition by giving it something, or harms it by killing it, merit or sin do not arise because an apparition does not have a mind that experiences pleasure or pain. Merit or sin occurs from benefiting or harming sentient beings whose minds are like magical apparitions because the benefit or harm causes their minds to experience pleasure or pain.

Because mantra, etc. lack the ability,

Arising from a variety of conditions,
A variety of magical apparitions also arise.

segments.translation_text: They may say: Even though on the ultimate level, the nature of all phenomena is emptiness and all phenomena naturally pass into nirvana, on the relative level, the cycle of birth, old age, illness, and death, etc. constitutes samsara. Therefore, those who have reached Buddhahood and ultimately entered nirvana would also become samsaric beings on the conventional level for the sake of other beings. So, what is the use of performing many hardships for the purpose of attaining such enlightenment? It would be meaningless.

segments.translation_text: Mind Only School: Madhyamika, your position is correct in its rejection of the Shravaka belief that external objects truly exist. However, if all phenomena were empty, then not even that delusion that holds the perception as real would exist. In that case, what intellect perceives the magical show? It would follow that there would be no knower to perceive it.

segments.translation_text: Mind Only School: Transparent crystal becomes blue in color depending on other conditions, but lapis lazuli and the like are naturally blue and do not depend on other conditions for their blueness. In the same way, vases and other objects are illuminated by a light, but light itself is naturally luminous and does not depend on other conditions to be illuminated. Because this can be seen by common sense, our example is not faulty.

segments.translation_html: Mind Only School: Transparent crystal becomes blue in color depending on other conditions, but lapis lazuli and the like are naturally blue and do not depend on other conditions for their blueness. In the same way, vases and other objects are illuminated by a light, but light itself is naturally luminous and does not depend on other conditions to be illuminated. Because this can be seen by common sense, our example is not faulty.

segments.translation_text: For example, you say that a light illuminates itself without depending on other conditions. Yet this can be said because it is recognized by the mind. Who perceives and describes this self-illumination? If you say that the mind perceives itself, then who is the perceiver of the perception? The evidence would become endless. Therefore self-perception is impossible. Perception by another mind is impossible because the mind of the past has already ceased, and the mind of the future has not yet arisen. With respect to the present mind, a commentary to the Pramana Virtika states:

segments.translation_text: Then, under careful analysis, the actual base of the mind itself cannot be perceived either by its own self awareness, or by another awareness. Therefore, descriptions of its unique qualities such as self-illumination like a light, or non self-illumination like a vase, etc., are merely descriptions of a non-existent base, like describing the elegance or size of the daughter of a barren woman. Though you say that the mind itself can be seen by its own awareness, because there is no evidence or proof, this statement has no meaningful result.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: If rigorously analyzed, phenomena have no true existence, yet they are perceivable. It is not necessary to reject the fact that on the worldly conventional level, phenomena can be directly perceived, or that phenomena can be indirectly perceived, such as by hearing quotations from the scripture, or understanding through logical imputation. It is not necessary because our school accepts on the relative level the things that worldly beings without rigorous analysis accept through consensus. However, the strong craving that adherents of your school feel for a consciousness that has true ultimate existence must be rejected, because that itself is the very cause of all suffering and defilements. Engaging in Suchness states:

segments.translation_text: Mind Only School: If consciousness did not truly exist in the ultimate sense, then the whole scheme of samsara and nirvana that is based on it would be invalid. Therefore, samsara, which is perceived in the manner of subject and object, has no true inherent nature. Yet the consciousness, which is free of duality, does have true material existence. Based on this, function becomes possible. Abandonment of that constitutes nirvana.

Even if it depended upon matter,
How could it possibly function?
Your mind alone without any assistant becomes isolated.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: In that case, if samsara were something other than truly materially existent, then it must be like space which is unable to function, and therefore, by implication, it is not matter. If samsara, which is perceived as dualistic, lacks material existence, then how could the activities of samsara possibly function based on non-dual material consciousness alone? It is like the inability of a rabbit’s horn to penetrate iron.

segments.translation_html:
Even if things are realized as magical apparitions,
How can the defilements be rejected?
Because toward a female magical apparition,
Lust arises even in her creator.

segments.translation_text: Mind Only School: Madhyamika, it is equally without benefit to realize that all phenomena are a magical apparition. Even if you know this, how is it possible to discard the defilements? It can be seen that they cannot be overcome. For example, when a magician creates a beautiful woman, not only do others feel lust for her, but even the magician who created her also feels lust even while knowing that she is a magical apparition.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: These cases are not similar. The creator of the magical woman himself has not abandoned clinging to phenomena as true, and also has not abandoned the obscuration of defilement, such as attachment, including habitual tendencies toward these obscurations. This is because when ordinary beings see an attractive woman, without analysis, lust toward her arises in the mind; their habitual tendencies toward emptiness are very weak.

segments.translation_text: Whereas, under careful analysis, all perceivable phenomena lack true existence. In stabilizing the habitual tendency toward realization of emptiness, initially the habitual tendency of strong clinging to matter is abandoned. Finally the lack of existence of all extremes, i.e. existence, nonexistence, etc., is realized. Becoming very familiar with this view, later even the habitual tendency of clinging to the extreme of emptiness is abandoned. Therefore it is said:

segments.translation_html:
When no material thing can be perceived
As the object of analysis,
Then how could non-matter, which is without foundation
Abide in the presence of the intellect?

segments.translation_text: Under careful analysis, if no material phenomena can be perceived, then nothing needs to be rejected or analyzed by saying that it has no truly existent nature. At that point, the very rejection of the absence of matter itself has no foundation or base. It cannot be perceived, like the death of the child of a barren woman. How could something possibly exist either before the mind, or in experienceable reality, because it has been demonstrated that nothing whatsoever exists?

segments.translation_text: When familiarization is completely accomplished, neither matter which has been rejected, nor non-matter, which has also been rejected, abide before the awareness as objects of experience. Then, as there is no third phenomenon other than these two, it is ascertained that there is no object whatsoever to be perceived. Just as fire does not appear if the fuel is exhausted, likewise, the intellect, or subject itself, becomes thoroughly calm and pacified if objects cease. Through this, the final relinquishment of nirvana is attained. The Madhyamika Avatara states:

segments.translation_text: One may wonder, "How can others’ welfare be accomplished if all conceptual thoughts are pacified?” An example is, even though precious wish-fulfilling jewels or wish-fulfilling trees have no conceptual thoughts, they fulfill every desire of living beings. Likewise, even though the dharmakaya, which is the ultimate accomplishment of relinquishment and realization, does not exert either effort or conceptual thought, the rupakaya is perceived according to capacities and motivations. This is due to the power of Buddhas’ previous aspirations as well as the fortune of disciples.

segments.translation_text: Likewise, during the stage of their training, Bodhisattvas performed the conduct that would attain great enlightenment and made aspirations that they would accomplish the welfare of sentient beings as long as samsara abides. Therefore, they accomplished the great sacred shrine of omniscient Buddhahood. Those practitioners long ago attained nirvana, the pacification of all forms of activity, yet due to the power of their previous aspirations, and disciples’ virtues, these Buddhas’ holy activities unceasingly accomplish the welfare of sentient beings.

segments.source_text: ཆོས་འཁོར་གནས་དང་ཡངས་པ་ཅན། ། ས་དཀར་ཅན་དང་ལྷ་ཡི་གནས། ། བྱིས་པ་གསོད་དང་ཀཽ་ཤམྦཱི། ། འབྲོག་གནས་མཆོད་རྟེན་རི་དང་ནི། ། འོད་མའི་ཚལ་དང་དགྲར་བཅས་དང༌། ། སེར་སྐྱ་ཡི་ནི་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ཏེ། ། འདི་རྣམས་སུ་ནི་ཐུབ་པ་ཡི། ། སྐྱེས་མཆོག་ལོ་རེ་ལོ་རེ་བཞུགས། ། འབར་བའི་ཕུག་གི་གནས་སུ་གཉིས། ། སྨན་གྱི་ནགས་སུ་ལོ་བཞི་སྟེ། ། རྒྱལ་པོའི་ཁབ་ཀྱི་གྲོང་དུ་ལྔ། ། དཀའ་བ་སྤྱད་པ་ལོ་དྲུག་སྟེ། ། ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་གསུམ་མཉན་ཡོད་དུ། ། ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་དགུ་ཁབ་གནས་སུ། ། དེ་ལྟར་རྒྱལ་བ་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་ལ། ། ཐུབ་མཆོག་དམ་པ་མྱ་ངན་འདས། །

segments.translation_text: The place where the wheel of Dharma was turned, Vaishali; White earth; the place of gods; The place where a child was killed; Kosambi; Place of nomads; mountain of stupas; Bamboo grove; place with enemies; and The city of Shravasti; In each of these holy places, the Great Sage, The excellent being, dwelt one year, and Two years in Blazing Cave; Four in Medicinal Forest; Five in Rajgir City; Six years at the place of austerity, Twenty-three in Shravasti, and Twenty-nine in his father’s kingdom. Thus, the Victorious One achieved eighty years And the Holy Sage entered nirvana.

segments.translation_text: Shravaka School: We ascertain that the four categories of scripture are the Buddha’s sermons because both you in the Mahayana school and we in the Shravaka school accept them as genuine scriptures. The Mahayana teachings are not the Buddha’s sermons because we do not accept them as genuine.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: This would imply that in the beginning, when others have not yet entered into trust in your scriptures, the four categories of scripture in your tradition could not be ascertained as the Buddhas’ sermons either, because those people do not accept them as genuine sermons.

segments.translation_text: Previously, you stated that a scripture is genuine if it is ascertained by both schools. However, the word "both” does not necessarily refer only to your school and ours; we are not the only schools. If the concurrence of two schools is what is required to ascertain that a scripture is genuine, then the texts that are mutually agreed upon by the Hindu Brahmins’ Four Vedas School and Rishi Kapila’s Long-Haired School would have to be considered as genuine as the Buddha’s sermons. But as this implication is outrageous, your reasoning about the authenticity of scripture is incorrect and it invalidates your challenge to the authenticity of the Mahayana teachings.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: Theravadin scriptures are also disputed by other schools, such as Hindu Logicians, and other non-Buddhists. Also, there are eighteen different schools within your own Theravadin tradition, and although the root is the same, you dispute with each other about the teachings. It follows that if the presence of dispute by other traditions were sufficient evidence to invalidate the scriptures, then your own schools’ scriptures would also be invalidated and need to be abandoned. However, if you do abandon them in this way, you would accumulate the bad karma of abandoning the holy Dharma and fall into the lower realms. The Ornament states:

segments.translation_text: The root of the wish-fulfilling tree of the Buddha’s doctrine is based upon the fully ordained who have conquered the defilements. From that arise the factors oriented toward enlightenment, like branches, flowers, and fruit. Even for such fully ordained, if the truth has been seen but emptiness has not been seen, then it will be impossible to conquer all defilements without exception, and it will be difficult to achieve even nirvana with remainder. Not only that, if the mind is not inclined toward emptiness, then it will be absorbed in clinging to matter, so it will be extremely difficult to attain nirvana without remainder of the aggregates.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: If that were the case, it would imply that immediately after the defilements have been abandoned and Arhathood attained, one is completely liberated from all forms of suffering. But this cannot be accepted because if they have not seen ultimate emptiness, even if the defilements are absent due to having been abandoned, the Arhats of the Lesser Vehicle are still seen to experience suffering as the ripening result of previous non-virtuous actions. For instance, a great disciple who attained Arhathood in Udrayana later experienced the suffering of being assassinated by someone from the city of Dadrok.

segments.translation_text: If profound emptiness is not realized, all perceptions are associated with clinging to matter as truly existent. segments.translation_text: Shravakas: Any speech that demonstrates the three precepts, such as being engaged with the sutra, observing the vinaya, and not contradicting the abhidharma, is part of the Buddha’s sermons. But the Mahayana teaching that everything is emptiness negates the three precepts, so it cannot be considered a sermon. Even if you say that a scripture states that without meditating emptiness, ultimate nirvana cannot be attained, that is not a trustworthy sermon.

segments.translation_text: In order to benefit those sentient beings experiencing a multitude of sufferings due to their delusion about the nature of samsara and nirvana, liberation from the extreme of attachment occurs by realizing emptiness through wisdom. Liberation from the extreme of peace occurs by not being afraid of suffering through compassion. Thus, non-abiding nirvana is attained. Having attained these two holy bodies as a base, holy activities continue uninterrupted until the end of samsara. This is the result of meditating on profound emptiness and benefiting sentient beings. The Mahayana Uttaratantra states:

Thus it is unsuitable
To criticize emptiness.
Therefore, without any doubt,
Meditate emptiness.

segments.translation_text: Thus, it is not suitable to criticize and reject profound emptiness by saying that it is not a sermon of the Buddha, and that its meaning is not the path, because if this teaching is abandoned, it will be impossible to attain ultimate liberation. Therefore, those who wish to attain ultimate nirvana should exert themselves without any doubt or hesitation, and with full trust in meditation on emptiness, as this is the ultimate path.

segments.translation_text: To explain in more detail, the obscuration of defilement hinders the attainment of liberation. The obscuration of cognition hinders the attainment of omniscience, as it obscures seeing suchness, and creates foggy darkness. Meditation on emptiness as its antidote is like an illuminating light. Therefore, why should those who wish to attain omniscient Buddhahood, which realizes the nature of all phenomena exactly and entirely, not meditate on this profound emptiness? By all means it is right to meditate on it.

segments.translation_html:
Toward matter, which produces suffering,
One should feel fear.
Toward emptiness, which pacifies suffering,
Why should one feel fear?

segments.translation_text: In fact, it is right to be terrified at the suffering of samsara which arises from clinging to matter. Samsara possesses many faults and it is right to be afraid of it. However, some are not afraid of those terrors, and instead are afraid of profound emptiness which has so many good qualities and pacifies all types of suffering, karma, and defilements. How could anyone be afraid of it? Being afraid is foolish and unsuitable.

segments.translation_html:
If there is something that is the so-called self,
One could feel fear toward any aspect of it.
There is no so-called self whatsoever,
So, who could feel that fear?

segments.translation_text: If either the personal or phenomenal self truly existed, then it would be possible to be afraid of something. However, under careful analysis, it is found that the so-called self does not exist whatsoever. So where is the one that is afraid? Nowhere can it be found. This reasoning is explained step by step.

segments.translation_text: On the relative level, everything can be perceived as impermanent, multiple, and dependent. On the ultimate level, they all lack any individual inherent nature. Therefore they are not the self. If the self were the same entity as the aggregates, then it would be subject to birth and disintegration. segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: If the self were the consciousness that perceives the five "just thatnesses,” such as sound, etc., this would imply that the self must exist at all times whether or not there is a sound, because the nature of the perceiver of sounds is permanent. But it would be impossible to prove it, because the perceiver of sound is explained on the basis of the existence of sound.

segments.translation_text: You Samkyai believe in raja, sattva, and tama, and when these three are in equilibrium, they are permanent and of the nature of the primordial substance, but they are not sentient beings. You believe that when they are in disequilibrium, they are sentient beings. Because the raja, sattva, and tama periodically change their shape, they are mere labels, like the example of father and son. But you believe that their prior and later natures are not different just as in the father and son example.

segments.translation_html:
You Samkyai believe in raja, sattva, and tama, and when these three are in equilibrium, they are permanent and of the nature of the primordial substance, but they are not sentient beings. You believe that when they are in disequilibrium, they are sentient beings. Because the raja, sattva, and tama periodically change their shape, they are mere labels, like the example of father and son. segments.translation_text: Not only that, it would also follow that the consciousness that you believe to be the self, and the primordial substance which lacks a mind, would be the same entity, because they are similar at the level of mere material existence. Further, when you believe that the parts of the consciousness do not truly exist as separate entities such as the perceiver of sound, and the perceiver of forms, etc., and that all of these are misconceptions, then what is this so-called "similarity at the level of mere recognition” that truly exists as the singular common foundation of all? This affirms that there is no such thing whatsoever.

segments.translation_text: Nayayika: Although the mind lacks any inherent nature, there is another mental substance that exists as the experiencer of objects.

segments.translation_text: Even if the self possesses mind, still it does not change the nature of awareness and cognition. Then how does that self that is a material substance and possesses other mental substances help to experience an object? Because nothing has been changed, it can’t contribute anything at all. Therefore it is contradictory to say that it is the experiencer of objects. Because it is material, it is not possible for it to be aware of objects, and if it is permanent, it must be free of all activity. If the self is all-pervasive, this would imply that even uncompounded space is the self, which is outrageous, so your position is disproved.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: It is not, because under analysis, the three times cannot be found. To explain this in detail, neither the past mind nor the future mind could be the self. This is because the past mind has already ceased, so it does not exist; the future mind is not yet born, so it does not yet exist. However, if you think that the present mind that is already born and has not yet ceased is the self, then once that disintegrates, there is no self. All compounded phenomena disintegrate immediately after they arise and do not abide without changing after the second moment.

segments.translation_text: In short, to use a metaphor, searching for the self is like peeling away the layers of bark from certain trees. No matter how many layers are peeled, the essential or inherent layer that is the tree is never found. Likewise, under careful analysis of the assembly of various aggregates that are separate entities, a truly existent self can never be found. Thus it is ascertained that on the ultimate level, no self exists.

segments.translation_text: To the childlike, the physical body is perceived as the material foundation of the self, feeling is the experience of matter by the self, mind is the material nature of the self, and phenomena are matter in both the deluded and thoroughly purified states. Since these are misconceptions, this teaching is given in order to abandon them.

segments.translation_text: As this explains, realize that this body is summarized by the suffering of the inferior compounded state; thus engage in completely realizing suffering. Realize that feeling is the cause of craving for all arising; thus engage in abandoning the all-arising defilements. Realize the mind as the base of clinging to the self; thus engage in manifesting cessation without fear of nirvana due to doubting that the self would be discontinued. Realize that phenomena are what need to be abandoned as they are defiled, and what needs to be adopted is complete freedom from them as the antidote; thus engage in meditation on the path without delusion. Thus engage in the four truths of the Noble One. Having engaged in them, one will be freed from a contaminated body, etc., and gradually attain all uncontaminated good qualities.

segments.translation_text: - Because it relies upon genuine wisdom which arises from study, contemplation and meditation on the vast and profound Dharma; - Likewise, it is a better antidote to the four misconceptions explained above because the purity, happiness, permanence, and nobility of the perfected self in the realm of reality are more exalted than the meditations on impurity, suffering, impermanence, and selflessness, which are still misconceptions compared to them; - Also because, as previously explained, others can also be gradually placed in the path, due to one’s own engagement in the four noble truths; - Because the bodies of all sentient beings are the object of observation, not only one’s own body; - Because of mental involvement in not perceiving anything, such as the body, etc., which is not only lack of clinging to the characteristics of matter; - Because of the attainment of non-abiding nirvana through not falling into the extreme of peace through freedom from a physical body, etc., and also not falling into the extreme of samsara through freedom; - Because it is harmonious with the six perfections, it is the antidote to their opposite factors such as miserliness, etc.; - Because of following according to the capacity of worldly beings, Shravakas, Prateka Buddhas, etc., the teachings are given according to their individual interests at that time; - Because of completely understanding that: the body is not genuine, but is perceived like a magical apparition; feelings are a mistaken conceptual experience, like a dream; the nature of mind is clear light, like space, and phenomena occur suddenly like clouds; - Because of attaining a birth completely free of defilements, they intentionally take birth as a universal monarch and attain a magnificent body a magnificent body and feelings; - Because their meditation is much greater than others, their natural intelligence is extremely sharp, so when they do even a little of the four contemplations of mindfulness, it is more exalted; - Because the merging and complete merging is more exalted, when the result is attained, they engage in harmonious motivation and application; - Because of possessing magnificent meditation which has inexhaustible good qualities even after attaining non-remaining nirvana; - Because of the perfect accomplishment of the temporary result of the Bodhisattva’s tenth bumi, and the final result of fully enlightened Buddhahood.

segments.translation_text: If the body is believed to be a single entity, then these are its multiple parts. Any one among them is not the body, because that would imply that if that part were defective, the body would disappear as in death. Thus, if you search each individual part, there is no place where the whole can be found. So where is the singular physical entity that we believe to be the whole body? This ascertains that nothing can be found.

If the entire body
Resides within its parts,
And within those parts also exist their own parts,
Then where does the body itself reside?

If you believe that a part of the body abides within each separate limb:

segments.translation_html:
If one's whole body
Resides in the hand and other parts,
There would be as many bodies as parts
Such as the hand, etc.

segments.translation_text: If a part of it abides in the individual limbs, such as the hand, etc., where is the whole body that is not divided into parts? If you analyze where it abides, there is no place where it exists. Therefore, it is ascertained that the body does not abide in its separate parts.

Thus the delusion that the whole abides in the parts is refuted.

segments.translation_text: If there is another body separate from the limbs, such as the hands, etc., it must be able to be perceived. As it cannot, it is proved that a whole singular body does not exist.

segments.translation_html:
Particles can also be split into atoms.
Even atoms can be split into directions.
Splitting the directions, one arrives at indivisible parts. 
These become like space, so atoms do not exist.

segments.translation_text: Just as under analysis, the whole body does not exist in the limbs, in the same way the hands and limbs are also merely the combination of smaller joints and body parts such as toes, fingers, etc. Hence there is no single entity that can be called a limb. A limb has no true existence.

segments.translation_text: The fingers are also a collection of various joints and smaller parts which also have no true existence. The smaller parts can be split into yet smaller parts such as top, bottom, etc. Under careful analysis, there is no whole that has a singular material existence. If those many smaller parts are in turn analyzed, they become as small as atoms, therefore no singular whole can be found. If atoms are analyzed, they are a collection of the six directions: north, south, east, west, zenith, and nadir, which are even smaller parts. The atom itself has no singular unitary existence.

segments.translation_text: Even a one-sixth portion of an atom can be split into six and then again six smaller parts, until finally it becomes like space. Since nothing exists, there is no nature of an indivisible atom which is the origin from which things are formed. segments.translation_text: If there is space between the organ such as the eye, and its object such as a form, then analyze where they meet. They do not meet or contact because there is space between them, like the space between a mountain in the north, and a mountain in the south. If there is no space between the two, it implies that they are a single entity. Thus, under careful analysis, what organ contacts which object? There is nothing, because both the meeting and the phenomena that meet do not exist.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: Those indivisible atoms do not meet each other in every direction, because one indivisible atom cannot merge with another atom. The reason is that the indivisible atoms have no empty space within them, and the atoms are supposed to be of equal size. Since these indivisible atoms cannot merge with each other, they cannot mix and without mixing, it is ascertained that there is no meeting. Without meeting, there is no contact. For this reason, it is ascertained that there is no feeling.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: Under careful analysis, who experiences the suffering? What is the harm? Because the feeler of suffering itself does not truly exist, then the feeling that is experienced also does not truly exist. Thus, under logical analysis based on reasoning on the ultimate level, it is ascertained that both the experiencer and the experience have no true existence. Once this is understood, how could the craving of searching for pleasure and avoiding pain not be rejected? It would certainly be rejected.

segments.translation_text: Again, the mind itself does not exist in the nature of the physical body. It does not exist in external material form other than the body. Nor does it exist as a mixture of the external and internal. There is no other place to search for the mind, and nothing can be found to truly exist. The conventional temporary mind itself cannot be found whatsoever under careful analysis. Because of that, and because of the unchanging nature of the ultimate, the nature of the minds of sentient beings is ascertained to be clear light, which is the essence of nirvana, the state beyond sorrow. The Mother of Perfection states:

segments.translation_html:
If the knower is prior to the known,
Upon what observation does it arise?
If the knower and known are simultaneous,
Upon what observation does it arise?

segments.translation_text: If the eye consciousness, etc. existed prior to the object (such as form), then by focusing on what object did the consciousness of that sense organ arise? The object of focus (form, etc.) does not exist because it has not yet arisen. If the eye consciousness, etc. arises simultaneously with the object (such as form), then by focusing on what object did that sense consciousness arise? There is none because simultaneous coexistence does not constitute cause and result.

segments.translation_html:
Thus, for those for whom the relative does not exist,
How could there possibly be two truths?
Also, if the relative is another entity.
How could sentient beings reach nirvana?

segments.wylie: gal te de ltar chos thams cad skye 'gags med pa yin na skye 'jig can gyi kun rdzob med par 'gyur bas/_de'i lugs la bden pa gnyis kyi rnam bzhag ga la yod de med par 'gyur zhing*/_bden gnyis su 'byed pa de yang kun rdzob ni gzhan 'khrul pa'i blo can gyis btags pa tsam gyis 'jog pa yin na/_'khrul snang ma 'gags pa'i sems can rnams mya ngan las ga la 'da' ste rang bzhin gyis mya ngan las 'das pa ma yin par 'gyur ro zhe na/_
segments.translation_text: They may say: Then, if all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing, that would imply that relative phenomena, which are subject to arising and disintegration, do not exist. So in such a tradition, how could there be a framework of two truths? There could not be. If the classification of two truths also constitutes a mere labeling of phenomena by a deluded mind on the relative level, then it would follow that sentient beings who have not ceased their delusions could not naturally enter nirvana.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: This is not a logical fault. For the time being, relative truth is other than nirvana and it constitutes deluded perception until conceptual thought ceases in the samsaric mind. If analyzed, nothing can be found that has existence. This is nirvana because the nature of nirvana is not these myriad conventional perceptions. It is the ultimate realm of reality, which abides unchangeably. The Buddha said:

segments.translation_html:
If there can be no father without a child,
What is the source of the child?
Without producing a child, one cannot be a father;
Thus, they are both nonexistent.

segments.translation_html:

Be understood from the knower?

segments.translation_text: They may reply: Even if something is dependent, it does not contradict its true existence. For example, a sprout arises dependent upon a seed. From the process of the birth of the sprout, the existence of the seed can be understood. In the same way, the knower arises from that which is known. Even though they are dependent, from the evidence of the existence of the subject which is the knower, why cannot the existence of the object which is the known, be realized? It certainly could.

They may reply: Even if something is dependent, it does not contradict its true existence. For example, a sprout arises dependent upon a seed. From the process of the birth of the sprout, the existence of the seed can be understood. In the same way, the knower arises from that which is known. segments.translation_html:
If a seed can be understood based on the sprout,
This is due to the knower who is separate.
From what source can one understand the existence
Of the knowing that understands that knowledge?

segments.translation_text: The understanding of a seed from a sprout is not due only to the sprout itself. The sprout must be perceived by a knower who is other than the sprout. Due to the certainty of an interconnection between the cause, which is a previous seed, and its result, then it is understood conceptually that the sprout had a previous seed as its cause.

Is generated by variation of causes.

For example, the colors and shapes of the stalk, branches, leaves, and flowers of a lotus are all produced by a variety of individual different causes.

segments.translation_text: However, under careful analysis, earth and the other four elements could not be Ishvara, as you believe, for the following reasons: You believe that Ishvara is singular, but there are multiple elements. You believe that Ishvara is permanent, but the elements are impermanent. You believe that Ishvara possesses a mind, yet the elements have no mind. You believe that Ishvara is a living god, but the elements are not a god, they are a material substance. You believe that Ishvara is the object of veneration, but we step on the elements, such as earth, with our feet and so they are not the object of veneration. You believe that Ishvara is a pure substance, yet the elements are polluted by feces, urine, and other impure substances. Because their characteristics are not similar, it is ascertained that the four elements could not be Ishvara.

segments.translation_text: If something depends upon other conditions, the cause of the result is the assembly of conditions, not Ishvara. segments.wylie: gzhan yang gal te dbang phyug de 'bras bu skyed par mi 'dod bzhin du rkyen tshogs pas 'bras bu skyed par byed na gzhan gyi dbang du thal bar 'gyur zhing*/_'on te dbang phyug gi 'dod pa las skye na'ang 'bras bu skye ba ni 'dod pa nyid la rag las par 'gyur bas/_de ltar 'dod pa'i dbang gis 'bras bu byed na rtag gcig rang dbang can gyi dbang phyug brtan g.yo thams cad kyi byed pa po ga la yin te ma yin par grub po/_/
segments.translation_text: If Ishvara does not intentionally desire to produce a result, he generates the result because conditions are assembled, which implies that Ishvara is dependent upon other power. However, if something arises from Ishvara’s intention, then production of the result depends upon intention. Thus, if his results are produced under the power of intention, how could Ishvara be permanent, singular, independent, and the creator of the container and contained? Hence it is ascertained that Ishvara is not the creator.

segments.translation_text: The nature of all phenomena is what is known as the three qualities of sattva, raja, and tama. The state of balance between pain, pleasure, and neutrality is the principal cause of the primordial substance. When these are not in balance, the temporary form aspect arises. Initially, an intellect, also known as a "giant” arises, which is like a very clear double-sided mirror. The person is inside the mirror and objects are outside the mirror. From the outside, objects appear like an image on the surface. When they mix, the person experiences the object. From this arises self pride and from that the five internal sense organs such as the eyes, etc., and the five action organs such as the mouth, hands, legs, genitals, and anus. The awareness organ is the nature of both of these. There are five just thatnesses, such as sound, etc. In total there are sixteen. From the five just thatnesses, arise the five elements, such as space, etc.

segments.translation_text: It is illogical to believe that the primordial substance is permanent, singular, and that it truly exists when the three qualities of raja, sattva, and tama are in balance because it is extremely contradictory to say that something is singular, yet composed of three things in balance. segments.translation_html:
Subtleness is the absence of grossness;
The occurrence of grossness and subtleness is impermanence.
Likewise, why wouldn’t we agree
That all matter is impermanent?

segments.translation_text: If it changes into multiple natures as the earlier gross form is set aside and later replaced by a subtle form, then its very appearance as gross and subtle is evidence of impermanence.
segments.translation_html: If it changes into multiple natures as the earlier gross form is set aside and later replaced by a subtle form, then its very appearance as gross and subtle is evidence of impermanence.

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: It is true that a result which does not clearly exist at the time of the cause does develop, even if your tradition does not accept it, because you have already agreed that things can clearly arise later, even if they do not clearly exist before. Also, on the level of mere perception, we can see that a result freshly arises from its cause, even if it was previously absent.

segments.wylie: dpyad na brdzun pa yin yang re zhig gnyen por 'gyur ba ni mi 'gal te dgag bya bum pa la sogs pa brtags pa'i dngos po la ma reg cing ma dpyad par/_de bkag pa yid dngos med 'dzin pa ni srid pa ma yin la/_dgag bya bden pa'i dngos po ma grub pa de'i phyir brdzun pa'i dngos po gang yin pa de bkag pa yid dngos med stong ba nyid kyang gsal bar brdzun pa nyid yin mod/_'on kyang de sgom pa ni 'thad de bden par 'dzin pa'i gnyen po byed pa'i phyir ro/_/
segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: Even though analysis shows it to be false, it is not contradictory for it to be a temporary antidote. For instance, without contacting and analyzing these material things such as vases, etc. that need to be rejected, it is impossible to cling to them as non-material. Since matter itself, which needs to be rejected, does not truly exist, then, by rejecting matter as false, emptiness, which is non-material, is also clearly false. However, it is suitable to meditate on it, because it acts as an antidote against the clinging that matter truly exists.

segments.translation_html:

segments.translation_text: Therefore, in a dream a son may be born and die. The conceptual thought, "Now the son does not exist because he is dead,” itself is the antidote to clinging to the existence of the son. It is not a contradiction to use such a counteracting conceptual thought, even though it is false.

segments.translation_html:
It does not come from another source,
Nor does it abide or go.
How is that which is imputed by delusion as truth
Different than a magical apparition?

segments.translation_text: Again, phenomena did not come from another time elsewhere to here, as some other traditions that hold that the three times do materially exist, may believe. segments.translation_text: Also, all resulting phenomena become perceivable when causes and conditions gather together closely. If causes and conditions are lacking, they will not be perceivable. Phenomena are like a temporary artificial image on the surface of a mirror. How could any interdependently arising perception have true existence in ultimate reality? None could. Because on the level of mere perception they are dependent on causes and conditions, realize that their nature is ultimately empty.

segments.wylie: gal te dngos po rnams yod pa kho na mtha' gcig tu bden par gyur bar 'dod na de la skyed byed kyi rgyu yis dgos pa ci zhig yod de yod par grub zin pa rnams rgyu la ltos pa med pa'i phyir ro/_/'on te dngos po de ni med pa kho na mtha' gcig tu nges na yang de la'ang rgyu yis dgos pa ci zhig yod de/_med pa ni rgyu rkyen gyis phan gdags byar ma grub pa'i phyir ro/_/
segments.translation_text: If it is believed that matter absolutely exists in reality, why does it need a cause to be produced? This is because existence means that its existence has already been accomplished, so it does not need to depend upon a cause. However, if it is certain that matter absolutely does not exist, in that case, why does it need a cause, because non-existence means that there is no base to be benefited by causes and conditions?

segments.translation_text: Madhyamika: That statement is illogical. Needless to say by a few causes, even by a hundred million causes, something that is not matter cannot ever be changed into matter. Further, by abandoning the state of non-matter, how could something change into matter? Under careful analysis, these are impossible.

If it is not separate from non-matter,

Because that would imply it would have two natures.

segments.wylie: dngos med kyi gnas skabs dang ni ma bral na'ang dngos po yod pa'i ngo bor 'gyur ba'i skabs mi srid pa'i phyir ro/_/dngos med dngos por mi 'gyur bar ma zad/_dngos po'ang dngos po med par nam yang 'gyur ba min te/_gal te 'gyur na dngos po gcig nyid sngar dngos por yod pa dang phyis dngos po med pa'i rang bzhin gnyis su bden par ha cang thal bar 'gyur ba las/_de lta bu ni mi srid pa'i phyir ro/_/
segments.translation_text: If it is not separate from the non-material state, it is impossible for there to be an opportunity for it to transform its nature into existent matter. Not only is it impossible for something non-material to become matter, it is also impossible for matter to become non-material. If it were to change, it would imply that the same thing could have two natures, which is outrageous, and that the same phenomena could first exist as matter and later become non-matter. Such things are impossible.

Or what is the use of feeling joy, delight and attachment at desirable occurrences? Since nothing has really occurred, give up adopting and discarding the eight worldly dharmas. segments.translation_text: Still they indulge again and again in a great heap of unwholesome actions which are the cause that produces more suffering in the future. Look upon these beings, who are unable to obtain the simple necessities of their lives, such as food and clothing, and who pursue their livelihoods with great hardship. Seeing that they dwell in the midst of great suffering, meditate great compassion focusing on them.

segments.translation_text: Throughout beginningless samsara, due to contaminated virtue, sentient beings are repeatedly born in the higher realms of humans and gods. They repeatedly indulge in a multitude of contaminated pleasures, such as the glory and wealth of kingdoms. However, they are unable to make these experiences fruitful, and come under the power of unwholesomeness when their life ends. When they transfer their life, they fall into the three lower realms, such as hell, etc., where they experience unbearable suffering for an extremely long period of time. Focusing on them, meditate great compassion.

segments.translation_text: While abiding there for a short time, due to wishing to be healthy and hoping to live a long life, beings are occupied with busy activities, such as bathing, applying ointments, taking medication, and the like. They suffer from poverty and destitution due to not finding food and clothing; weariness and turmoil from activities associated with their livelihood; confusion due to sluggishness and sleep; and harm due to challengers and wildness. Likewise, due to association with ordinary childlike beings, life becomes fruitless through praising themselves, blaming others, etc. Thus life passes swiftly.

segments.wylie: de nas slar [p.-383] [[rab gsal snang ba]] yang mi khom pa'i gnas spang ba'i dal ba phun sum tshogs pa rnyed par dka' zhing sangs rgyas 'byung ba la sogs pa'i 'byor ba phun sum tshogs pa'ang rnyed pa shin tu dka' la/_de dag rnyed kyang 'dod chags la sogs pa'i nyon mongs pa 'khor ba ngan song gi rgyun phyogs su 'khyer bar phyed pas chu bo chen po dang 'dra ba rnams na spang bar dka' ste e ma sdug bsngal drag po myong bzhin du nyon mongs pa'i dbang gis las ngan pa spyad de/_slar yang sdug bsngal rgyun mi 'chad par khor yug tu brgyud pas myong bar 'gyur ba 'di dag ni shin tu snying rje ba nyid do/_/
segments.translation_text: It is difficult to find the perfect opportunity of leisure that is free of unfavorable conditions. Also, it is extremely difficult to find the opportunity of endowment, such as the appearance of the Buddha and the like. Even if it is attained, the great torrent of defilements, such as attachment, etc. drags beings toward samsara and lower rebirth, so it is difficult to abandon them. Alas! While experiencing severe suffering, still they continue to indulge in evil karma, under the power of defilements. Again they will experience suffering in a constant, unbroken continuum, like the turning of a wheel. How pitiful is the condition of these beings!

segments.translation_html: It is difficult to find the perfect opportunity of leisure that is free of unfavorable conditions. Also, it is extremely difficult to find the opportunity of endowment, such as the appearance of the Buddha and the like. Even if it is attained, the great torrent of defilements, such as attachment, etc. drags beings toward samsara and lower rebirth, so it is difficult to abandon them. Alas! While experiencing severe suffering, still they continue to indulge in evil karma, under the power of defilements. Again they will experience suffering in a constant, unbroken continuum, like the turning of a wheel. How pitiful is the condition of these beings!

segments.translation_text: As explained above, even though beings dwell in the midst of a multitude of different types of severe suffering, their eye of primordial wisdom is obscured by the cataract of ignorance, and they are unable to see that they dwell in suffering. Such sentient beings dwell sunken in the great rivers of the sufferings of birth, old age, illness, and death. Alas! They are so pitiful that it is suitable to mourn for them, because they are dominated by clinging to the misperception of suffering as pleasure.

segments.translation_text: As has been explained step by step above, they are unaware that the nature of all compounded phenomena is impermanence. As a result, they live as if old age, which is changing of youth, and death which is the changing of life will never occur. While they are heedlessly indulging in excessive pleasure, first, old age and illness occur, and later, in an inevitable manner, death arrives and they are slaughtered and again fall into the lower realms where they experience unbearable suffering that destroys them. Therefore, they are the objects of great compassion. The sutra Advice to the King states:

segments.translation_text: Great King, old age will come with the diminishing of youth: illness will come with the diminishing of health: decline will come with the diminishing of success: death will come with the diminishing of life. There is no place to escape from these by swiftly running away: they cannot be repelled by power: nor can wealth be a ransom. They are not easy to pacify by other methods such as medicine, mantra, magical substances, etc.

segments.translation_text: As explained above, for a long time, sentient beings experience the fires of myriad sufferings such as heat and cold, being cut and slashed, hunger and thirst, turmoil and weariness, etc. Aspire that those sentient beings may attain higher rebirth thinking, "When can I become an agent, who accumulates the cause of happiness by gathering a vast heap of merit like a cloud, from which falls a continuous rain of clothing, ornaments, food, wealth, etc. to provide happiness and benefit to each of them?” Thus wish to pacify their suffering and place them in happiness.

segments.translation_html:
When will I be able to teach emptiness
To those who struggle with objects,
Through my devoted accumulation
Of objectless merit?

segments.translation_text: Aspire that they may attain liberation which is ultimate excellence, by wishing, "When can those sentient beings have a motivation that does not perceive the three cycles, an application that accumulates a great heap of merit, and the result of the attainment of Buddhahood? Then, having attained Buddhahood, teach the profound Dharma of ultimate emptiness to those sentient beings who have the view of material clinging, and strong clinging to objects which obscures their minds, that they may practice the Dharma according to what has been taught, and swiftly attain great enlightenment.”

segments.translation_text: Thus, those who wish to attain higher rebirth and excellent ultimate liberation engage in virtues that arise from giving, morality, and meditation.
